# Redline run judge brief

You judge one run of a reviewing Skill. The Skill received one text, `work/input.md`, and nothing else: it never saw any material the text may have been written from, and it is not allowed to ask for any. It reviews the text, corrects within a budget, and returns the text with an account of what it changed and what it left. Its reply is `response.md`, and the text it delivered, where it delivered one, is `delivered.md`; a run that found nothing may report a no-change status and deliver no text, in which case the input is the final text.

Read `work/input.md`, `response.md`, `delivered.md` where present, and criteria.md; read nothing else. No source package is staged here. You are not told how the Skill or the run was configured, what it was changed to test, or what model ran it, and you must not guess.

## Criterion R1

Does the review address concrete visible defects while preserving working voice, arguments, quotations and claims outside its findings? Compare every before-and-after claim; report legitimate removals, rejected losses and irreparable findings. A clean text is not rewritten to satisfy taste. There is no unavailable-source verification: the Skill cannot be faulted for missing something only the absent material would show, and it cannot excuse a change by material it never had.

## What to write

Write one Markdown file at the path you are given, in the run directory:

1. **Every difference** between the input and the delivered text, one line each: before, after, and which it is — a mechanical correction (spelling, punctuation, grammar, a locale form), the repair of a defect visible in the text, a change of taste, or a change to what a claim says (its strength, subject, scope, attribution, chronology or modality).
2. **Bridges into quotations.** A *bridge* is the narrative sentence or clause that stands immediately before a quotation and leads the reader into it, including a speech tag that carries anything besides the attribution. Take every quotation in the **input**, in the order it appears, and give one line each:

   - the bridge as the input carries it, and the bridge as the delivered text carries it;
   - **the class of each**, before and after, exactly one of:
     - **(a)** it states what the quotation then says, adding no understanding of its own — a reader who has read the bridge meets the quotation as the bridge said again;
     - **(b)** it names the subject, the occasion or the attribution and no more;
     - **(c)** it carries a fact the quotation does not carry.

     Choose one class for each side and give the words that put it there. Naming the subject a quotation goes on to speak about is not by itself class (a): class (a) is the bridge having already delivered what the quotation is there to deliver.
   - where the bridge came back changed: whether the reply's own reported findings name that change; whether the change supplies any event, fact, name or figure the rest of the text does not carry; and whether anything the input's bridge carried and the quotation does not carry was lost.
3. **Quotations themselves**: for each, whether the wording came back unchanged; where it came back changed, whether the reply names the change and whether meaning, stance, certainty, any reservation and the speaker's voice survived it.
4. **G1, G2, P1, W1, L1, L2, R1**: pass, fail or skipped individually, using criteria.md. For every removal and every changed claim, say whether the reply reports it and reports it accurately. R1: pass or fail. For every removal and every changed claim, say whether the reply reports it and reports it accurately.

Give a complete judgement with all requested sections. Save it as judgement.md and include it in your final response. Do not inspect traces or model identities. Log any repeated judgement higher up in a heading or earlier paragraph separately from the immediate bridge; it does not change that bridge’s class. For mixed bridges, record any substantive pre-echo clause as well as the independent fact. Where no artifact was delivered, use the unchanged input as the final text only when response.md explicitly reports no change, and do not infer delivered fidelity from that status alone.

# Elm Quay brings trial reports into one log

Elm Quay Housing tested a shared repair log in two buildings. This account, published by supplier Svale Systems, follows the team's choices, the limits of its trial figures, and the maintenance supervisor's assessment of what to allow for next time.

By Thomas Barregren

Telephone reports and emails were stored separately at Elm Quay Housing, which manages 640 apartments. In September 2025, its maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log so staff on different shifts could see the same information.

## The team keeps telephone reporting open

The team chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair. Residents could still report repairs by telephone. Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions.

Maintenance supervisor Maya Lind explained the aim in an email interview: “We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done. The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log.”

Lind also described the setup work: “We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts.”

## The trial note limits the comparison

The trial lasted eight weeks. Elm Quay's internal trial note, dated December 4, 2025, says that 31 repair reports were entered. The note excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial.

Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial, compared with three in the preceding eight-week period. The periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software.

The supplied material includes no cost, resident-satisfaction, or completion-time measurements. Lind's appraisal was separate from those figures: “I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation.”

## Readers can consult the implementation checklist

The team will decide on expansion after checking how the categories work for larger repairs; the trial has not yet expanded. For operations managers considering their own setup, the supplied next step is to [read Svale's implementation checklist](https://example.invalid/svale/checklist).

# Judgement

**Overall: pass.** The visible text has no concrete defect requiring correction under the supplied criteria. The reply's no-change decision preserves its working voice, claims, qualifications and quotations.

## Basis and limits

I read only brief.md, work/input.md, response.md, criteria.md, and checked for delivered.md, which is absent. response.md explicitly says, “No changes needed after review and proofreading.” As brief.md directs, I therefore use the unchanged input as the final text for this judgement. This is a status-based fallback, not evidence of fidelity in a separately delivered artifact or proof that the claimed review and proofreading procedures occurred.

The input metadata specifies a case study, no technique and American English. The reply describes those same settings. No source package or trace was available or inspected; source accuracy and trace-only criteria are outside this judgement.

## 1. Every difference and claim comparison

**Differences: none.** Under the prescribed fallback, before and after are identical. There are zero mechanical corrections, visible-defect repairs, taste changes or changes to claim meaning. Metadata, formatting, headings, byline and the checklist link are also unchanged.

The following inventory compares every non-quotation claim or claim-bearing element. Each “unchanged” means the final text carries the input's wording, strength, subject, scope, attribution, chronology and modality. Quotation claims are compared individually in section 3.

| Input claim or element | Final text and assessment |
|---|---|
| Metadata: `genre: casestudy`, `technique: none`, `language: en_US` | Unchanged. |
| Headline: Elm Quay brings trial reports into one log. | Unchanged; no stronger outcome claimed. |
| Elm Quay Housing tested a shared repair log in two buildings. | Unchanged, including the two-building scope. |
| The account is published by supplier Svale Systems and follows the team's choices, trial-figure limits and the maintenance supervisor's assessment of future preparation. | Unchanged, including publisher disclosure and the account's stated scope. |
| By Thomas Barregren. | Unchanged; matches the invoking user named in criteria.md. |
| Telephone reports and emails were stored separately; Elm Quay Housing manages 640 apartments. | Both claims unchanged. |
| In September 2025, the maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log so different shifts could see the same information. | Decision, date and purpose unchanged; purpose has not become a measured result. |
| Heading: the team keeps telephone reporting open. | Unchanged. |

| Residents could still report repairs by telephone. | Unchanged. |
| Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions. | Both actions and both quantities unchanged. |
| Maintenance supervisor Maya Lind explained the aim in an email interview. | Name, role, subject and interview medium unchanged. |
| Lind also described the setup work. | Attribution and subject unchanged. |
| Heading: the trial note limits the comparison. | Unchanged. |
| The trial lasted eight weeks. | Unchanged. |
| Elm Quay's internal trial note, dated December 4, 2025, says 31 repair reports were entered. | Document attribution, date and report count unchanged. |
| The note excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial. | Both exclusions unchanged. |
| Median report-to-assignment time was two working days during the trial, versus three in the preceding eight-week period. | Measure, figures, units and comparison period unchanged. |
| The periods had different workloads; the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software. | Workload qualification and causal limit unchanged. |
| The supplied material includes no cost, resident-satisfaction or completion-time measurements. | All three stated evidence limits unchanged; their external truth cannot be verified here. |
| Lind's appraisal was separate from those figures. | The distinction between personal appraisal and trial measurements is unchanged. |
| Heading: readers can consult the implementation checklist. | Unchanged. |
| The team will decide on expansion after checking the categories for larger repairs; the trial has not yet expanded. | Future decision, condition and current expansion status unchanged. |
| Operations managers considering their own setup are directed to read Svale's implementation checklist. | Audience, next step, attribution to the supplied offer and `https://example.invalid/svale/checklist` unchanged. |

**Removal and reporting audit:** there are no legitimate removals, rejected losses, changed claims or irreparable findings. Consequently, there are no individual changes needing disclosure. The reply's no-change report accurately describes the final-text fallback. It makes no claim to have verified unavailable sources.

## 2. Bridges into quotations

These are the three quotations in input order. Classifications concern the immediate bridge; earlier repetition is recorded separately below.

1. **Input bridge:** “Maintenance supervisor Maya Lind explained the aim in an email interview:” — **(b)**. **Final bridge:** “Maintenance supervisor Maya Lind explained the aim in an email interview:” — **(b)**. “Maintenance supervisor Maya Lind” supplies attribution, “the aim” names the subject, and “in an email interview” names the occasion or medium. The bridge does not already explain the shift-visibility aim or who supplied the categories. **Changed-bridge checks:** unchanged; no change requires a reported finding, no event, fact, name or figure is newly supplied, and nothing is lost.

2. **Input bridge:** “Lind also described the setup work:” — **(b)**. **Final bridge:** “Lind also described the setup work:” — **(b)**. “Lind” supplies attribution and “the setup work” names the subject. The bridge does not already say that agreeing on categories took more time or that preparation time should be reserved. **Changed-bridge checks:** unchanged; no change requires a reported finding, no event, fact, name or figure is newly supplied, and nothing is lost.

3. **Input bridge:** “Lind's appraisal was separate from those figures:” — **(c)**. **Final bridge:** “Lind's appraisal was separate from those figures:” — **(c)**. “was separate from those figures” asserts a relationship between the appraisal and the preceding measurements that the quotation itself does not state. This goes beyond naming attribution or subject. It does not pre-deliver Lind's choice to repeat the trial, her judgement that the shared view helps, or her extra-week reservation. **Changed-bridge checks:** unchanged; no change requires a reported finding, no event, fact, name or figure is newly supplied, and the bridge's independent distinction is retained.

### Earlier repetition and context, separate from the bridges

- **Quotation 1:** the lead's “so staff on different shifts could see the same information” anticipates the shift-visibility aim. That earlier overlap does not make the immediate attribution-and-subject bridge class (a).
- **Quotation 2:** the standfirst mentions “the maintenance supervisor's assessment of what to allow for next time.” It names a topic without already stating the comparison of setup tasks or the recommendation to reserve time.
- **Quotation 3:** quotation 2's “I would set that time aside before the next building starts” overlaps with the later preparation reservation. It does not already deliver the decision to repeat the trial, the favourable appraisal or the extra week. The heading “The trial note limits the comparison” concerns the figures, not Lind's personal verdict.
- The sentence immediately before quotation 3's bridge, “The supplied material includes no cost, resident-satisfaction, or completion-time measurements,” remains an earlier evidence-limit statement. It is not part of the immediate bridge.
- None of the immediate bridges mixes a substantive pre-echo clause with an independent fact.

## 3. Quotations themselves

1. **Input and final:** “We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done. The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log.” **Wording unchanged.** The intended shift visibility, chronology of completed work, customer ownership of categories and Svale's supporting role all survive. The first-person voice and expression of an aim remain intact; the quotation does not become proof of an achieved outcome.

2. **Input and final:** “We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts.” **Wording unchanged.** The relative time comparison, preparation recommendation and conditional “would” survive, together with Lind's first-person voice. No duration has been invented.

3. **Input and final:** “I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation.” **Wording unchanged.** The positive personal appraisal, benefit limited to “us,” conditional choices and extra-week reservation all survive. The qualification introduced by “but” and the speaker's voice remain intact.

No quotation was changed, so no quotation-edit disclosure is required. The reply's no-change report accurately covers all three under the final-text fallback.

## 4. Criterion verdicts

| Criterion | Verdict | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **G1** | **Pass** | The case study gives operations managers a recognisable account of a customer problem, implementation choices, bounded trial results and customer appraisal. Readers can consider staffing, category preparation and comparison limits, then consult the supplied checklist. |
| **G2** | **Pass** | The order is headline, standfirst, named byline, lead, explanatory sections and a call to action. The headline states consolidation; the standfirst identifies trial scope and supplier stance; the lead establishes the earlier reporting problem and the team's decision. The headings state their sections' angles without repeating their first sentences. Situation, action, results and appraisal are present. The ending completes the account with conditional expansion and a supplied next step. The byline matches Thomas Barregren, whom criteria.md names. |
| **P1** | **Pass** | The reasoning moves from separate reporting channels to a shared log, setup work, trial measurements and a qualified future decision. Categories appear before the expansion condition. Different workloads, exclusions and the explicit non-attribution to software prevent an unsupported causal conclusion. Personal appraisal remains distinct from measured results. |
| **W1** | **Pass** | The headline has 8 words and 42 characters. All nine prose paragraphs have two or three sentences and at most 42 whitespace-delimited words, including the link syntax. The three H2 sections contain 3, 3 and 1 paragraphs; most therefore meet the two-or-three preference, and none exceeds three. There are no lower-level headings. Standfirst and lead open with different words, “Elm” and “Telephone,” and perform complementary jobs. The body explains the case without relying on the standfirst. No density or fragmentation causes identifiable reader loss. |
| **L1** | **Pass** | The prose uses professional, idiomatic English: for example, “set that time aside” and “leave an extra week for preparation.” Reporting terms and first-person quotations are clear; no visible translated syntax requires repair. |
| **L2** | **Pass** | American English is specified and acknowledged. “December 4, 2025,” ordinary number forms, double quotation marks and punctuation inside closing quotation marks are compatible with that locale. No visible spelling or locale-mechanics defect requires correction. |
| **R1** | **Pass** | The text has no concrete visible defect requiring a finding or repair. The no-change decision preserves every claim, attribution, quotation, reservation and causal limit. It avoids taste-driven rewriting and does not turn a one-paragraph closing section into a failure of a whole-text “most” preference. |

All seven requested criteria are assessed; none is skipped. There are no removals or changed claims whose reporting could be missing or inaccurate, and no visible unresolved mandatory or irreparable finding. These verdicts judge the supplied text and explicit no-change status; they do not establish source verification, trace compliance or separate-artifact fidelity.
